title: Topaz Video AI MCP Server: Setup Guide (2026)
summary: Topaz Video AI MCP merges MCP protocol with Topaz's video tool. You'll understand what actually exists and whether it fits your workflow.
body_markdown:
## Batch enhancement jobs with Activepieces


Whatever Topaz costs you, Activepieces adds nothing to the enhancement itself: it's an automation layer that hands files to the Topaz job on your machine and reports what happened. It has no upscaling models, and it can't make a Topaz result better or faster.


What it does add is no cap on the number of flows, since every plan, including free, allows unlimited flows, and the free plan on Activepieces Cloud comes with 1,000 credits a month.


### Trigger on new files


To start a flow, Activepieces needs a trigger, and the one I would use is the webhook. A small script on the Topaz machine watches the input folder and posts the new file's path to the flow when something lands.


Don't assume Activepieces can watch your local disk by itself, since the flow runs wherever it is hosted.


The free self-hosted Community Edition is the MIT-licensed core, so it can run on your own infrastructure next to the Topaz machine, but the watcher is still a few lines of your own code, and it's the part that breaks first if the machine sleeps or the folder is renamed.


### Run the job and report back


In the middle of the flow sits a call into Topaz's command-line tools, through a script on the Topaz machine or an HTTP endpoint you put in front of one. Topaz does the enhancement there, using its own models and your settings.


Activepieces only waits for the result, then moves the output to a delivery folder or sends a message. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production, so this waiting-and-reporting step is not an exotic use of it.


Before announcing success, check the exit status of the job, because a flow that reports "done" on a failed render is worse than no flow at all.


Activepieces only knows the Topaz settings you pass into the flow, so log them yourself; the extra step costs nothing more, since a run is 1 credit however many steps it has.


> Before announcing success, check the exit status of the job, because a flow that reports "done" on a failed render is worse than no flow at all.


### Expose one approved workflow over MCP


This is the hosted counterpart to writing your own server, and it's not a Topaz feature: Activepieces runs a per-project MCP server that a client such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor can call, and MCPs are included on the free plan.


I would expose exactly one flow: the tested one that takes a file and returns an enhanced copy with fixed settings.


Leave out anything that lets a model choose arbitrary commands. Confirm the current setup steps in the Integrations Framework and MCP Server documentation rather than relying on my description, because this part of the product changes quickly.


To see why that restraint is practical, look at the version history panel below. It lists two saved versions of a webhook flow, each with a timestamp and status marker, and the flow itself is a webhook trigger, a code step and an end.


The takeaway is that you can see which revision you tested before you expose it.


Once you've picked the version you trust, treat it as frozen. Make changes in a new version, so the tool your assistant calls is never one you're still editing.
